artworks.title: The Mutilation of Uranus by Saturn
artworks.description: Fresco by Giorgio Vasari and Cristofano Gherardi in the Palazzo Vecchio, Florence. It depicts the primal act of the succession myth as told in Hesiod's Theogony: Saturn (Cronus) wields the sickle against his father Uranus, the primordial sky, ending the sky-god's reign over the cosmos.

artworks.title: Aion–Uranus in the Zodiac Wheel (mosaic)
artworks.description: Roman floor mosaic from Sentinum in Italy, now in the Glyptothek in Munich. The youthful god of eternal time, Aion — here identified with Uranus as lord of the heavens — stands inside the wheel of the zodiac, while the earth goddess reclines below with her children, the seasons.

artworks.title: Uranus and the Dance of the Stars
artworks.description: Schinkel's Romantic sky-father: Ouranos enthroned among circling constellations — the primordial heaven as architecture of light rather than Hesiod's wounded giant.

artworks.title: Cronus Castrating Uranus
artworks.description: A French Renaissance miniature of the Theogony's founding crime: Cronus raises the sickle against Uranus — Heaven cut from Earth at the dawn of the Titans.

artworks.title: Castration of Uranus
artworks.artist: After Polidoro da Caravaggio, retouched by Peter Paul Rubens
artworks.description: A drawing after Polidoro's Roman façade invention, later touched by Rubens: Saturn's assault on the sky-god — the succession myth circulating as a collector's sheet.

popCulture.title: Uranus
popCulture.description: Herschel's seventh planet took the sky-father's name — Ouranos among the planets, after the Roman gods had claimed the nearer skies.
